title: Keep your color
hook: whatever anyone does, I must be good, as an emerald keeps its color (Meditations 7.15)

segments.voice: Yesterday: member, not part, the single letter between a spare piece and a living limb. Your line was a member. Who did you help like family? The week ends today, so we'll look back. Day five hundred eighty-eight.

Drop an emerald in mud. Rinse it. Green. Leave it in a dark drawer for a hundred years. Green. Insult it, praise it, sell it, steal it, put it in a crown or a junk shop. Still green. It doesn't change color depending on who's holding it. People are not like that. We go a little gray around gloomy people, a little sharp around sharp ones. Marcus Aurelius wanted to be more like the stone.
screen: `AN EMERALD IN MUD.` → `STILL GREEN.` → `PEOPLE CHANGE COLOR.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Meditations seven, fifteen. Whatever anyone does or says, Marcus writes, I must be good. Just as gold, or an emerald, or purple dye might always be saying: whatever anyone does or says, in George Long's translation, "I must be emerald and keep my colour." Second, why those three. Gold, emerald, and purple were the ancient world's luxury goods. Purple dye was famous because it didn't fade, and gold doesn't tarnish. Marcus picks things whose whole value is that they stay what they are. An emerald that turned brown when someone was rude to it wouldn't be worth much. Third, the shift in responsibility. Notice the sentence begins with whatever anyone does or says. Marcus isn't hoping for kinder people. He takes their behavior as unpredictable. Then he moves all the responsibility to the one thing that's his: I must be good. Your goodness isn't a reaction. It's your color. Fourth, the week. Look back at what this week asked. Love the people you're with. Honor the dead philosophers. Principles live, and can be rekindled. Stay good-natured in the idle show. Treat the bond as holy. Be a member, not a part. And now, keep your color. It's the week of other people, really. Seven ways of staying yourself among them. Not hard and cold, like a stone that shuts people out. Clear and steady, like a stone the light passes through.
screen: `I MUST BE EMERALD.` · `GOLD, EMERALD, PURPLE.` · `WHATEVER ANYONE DOES, I MUST BE GOOD.` · `THIS WEEK: STAYING YOURSELF.` · then, large: `KEEP MY COLOR.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think of a person who tends to change your color. Someone whose mood darkens yours, or whose sharpness makes you sharp. Picture being with them. Notice the familiar shift beginning. Now picture an emerald in your palm, cool and green. Imagine staying exactly your own shade of kind while they are whatever they are. No need to change them. Just keep your color. The bell holds the time.
Keep your color. Marcus's emerald, which stays green whatever anyone does or says. Today's word.
Your line: keep my color. When someone provokes you today, picture the emerald, say the line, and stay good in your own shade. Day five hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often picture the emerald when they're provoked, as a reminder that their own goodness doesn't depend on how others behave.

trapdoor: what you thought: be tough and unaffected, like a rock.
what it means: stay good whatever others do, the way an emerald stays green, clear rather than cold.
what a scholar hears: purple dye from murex shells was prized precisely for not fading, which is why Marcus pairs it with gold and emerald.
